newsitem.title: CHINA: China issues new rules on stock exchanges.
newsitem.headline: China issues new rules on stock exchanges.

text.p: China on Friday promulgated a new set of stock market regulations, removing from local governments the power to manage and supervise markets and giving the power to the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC).

The rules, published by the Shanghai Securities News on Friday, come into effect immediately and replace an old set of rules issued on July 7, 1993, which empowered the CSRC to supervise the exchanges and local governments to manage them.
China has two bourses, in Shanghai and Shenzhen. Beijing has said that it will not set up a third one in the near future.
The new rules added provisions to strengthen supervision of the exchanges.
The exchanges should not do business for profits, publish newspapers and magazines, make predictions of market movements and offer credit or guarantees to others, the rules said.

The rules said the exchanges should order an immediate suspension of shares of listed companies if extraordinary situations occur such as abnormal price movements of their shares, takeover announcements by a third party or a request by a listed firm to suspend trading.
The new rules added a chapter governing stock-clearing institutions, requiring such bodies to have a minimum registered capital of 100 million yuan.

A clearing house registers and takes care of stocks for investors and settles accounts for customers and all its documents should be kept for a certain period and some important ones should not be destroyed for 20 years, the rules said.

The rules said exchange chairmen and general managers and their deputies should be nominated by the CSRC and then, after consultations with local governments, can be appointed by the boards of directors of the exchanges.
The Securities Commission under the State Council, the Cabinet, said the rules had been revised after years of changes had made the old ones out-of-date.

"Whether the exchanges can play a self-disciplinary role will directly affect the standardisation and development of the stock market," it said. "Supervision of the exchanges is a basic pre-condition and an important part of stock market management."
The commission said the exchanges should learn lessons from episodes such as a major treasury bill futures scandal in February last year on the Shanghai stock exchange.
